Posted July 11, 2002
Analysis by Richard Cowan

We are winning!

As long anticipated, cannabis possession will soon be a " non-arrestable offense " in the UK. The police will still seize the cannabis and issue a warning, but not arrest people for personal possession.

This policy change is likely to have a major impact in Canada, and some other countries in the Commonwealth. It was even reported in

As is usually the case with cannabis reform, it was not done with any real knowledge of or concern about -- the cannabis community. So the " new policy " is a muddle that pleases no one. But that is not all bad.

Although it would be best for the prohibitionists to do the right thing, pause for laughter, the second best is for them to make fools of themselves in retreat. They have definitely done that!

As the time approached for Home Secretary David Blunkett to confirm the details of the Blair government's new cannabis policies, the comments from the media, police and politicians became so absurd that I started filing them under a new category: " bonkers. "
For an example see

That also turned out to be the one description of the new policy that everyone outside of the government might agree on.

First, let's try to sort out what the new policy really means.

There are three " classes " of illegal drugs under UK law.

Class A: Heroin, cocaine, ecstasy, LSD, and injectable amphetamines. Maximum sentence for dealing is life and seven years for possession.

Class B: Currently includes cannabis, amphetamines and barbiturates. The maximum sentence for dealing is 14 years in prison plus a fine, and for possession it is five years plus fine.

Class C: Will include cannabis next July, but now includes anabolic steroids, anti-depressants (benzodiazepines like Valium) and growth hormones. Maximum sentences for dealing in Class C substances are to be increased from five years to 14. The maximum term for possession is two years in jail, although we are assured that almost no one will really be prosecuted for cannabis possession.

Unfortunately, there is no set quantity defined as " personal " as of yet.

Although the government has the power to reclassify cannabis from Class B to Class C without a Parliamentary vote, Blunkett decided that he wants to make changes in the law, not just reclassify it. This means that the law will not be formally changed until next summer, at the earliest.

As noted, he wants to raise the maximum penalty for selling Class C drugs raised from 5 to 14 years, the same as for heroin. As Deborah Orr said in The Independent, " The link between cannabis and harder drugs is procedural rather than intrinsic, and much exacerbated by the necessity of the customer to enter a market just as illegal for cannabis as it is for crack. By increasing penalties for cannabis dealing, the Government would be encouraging this problem, rather than intervening against it.

By classifying cannabis dealing alongside violent assault and gun crime, as the new legislation will, the incentive to stick with cannabis dealing and stay away from hard-drug dealing will be severely eroded. Cannabis is more likely than ever to be sold alongside hard drugs by people who consider themselves to be professional criminals, rather than by soft-drug dealers who often see themselves as freedom fighters and put-upon campaigners for civil liberties. "

(Orr did an excellent job, and even mentions that Colin Davies is being held in Strangeways prison. The first time that this has been reported in a major UK paper!

Colin's hearing has been delayed until tomorrow.)

Second, Blunkett bowed to police pressure, and cannabis possession will not always be a non-arrestable offense. He wants to have a hybrid system, under which police could arrest some people caught with cannabis under certain circumstances.

Those who smoke cannabis near a school or in a public place where other people object to their smoking could still be arrested. Neither of these powers seems terribly objectionable, but could easily be abused. For example, this provision could apply to people who take part in civil disobedience demonstrations.

The problem with giving the police discretion was illustrated by a study by the Joseph Rowntree Foundation that showed that 3 per cent of police officers were responsible for 20 per cent of cannabis possession arrests. These prohibitionist ideologues are pursuing a personal crusade against cannabis.

Will they abuse their discretionary powers?

However, as noted, these changes in the law will not go into effect for a year. In the meantime, the police are trying to come up with an interim policy. The Association of Chief Police Officers is working on national guidelines that will be an extension of the Brixton " seize and warn " experiment, but these will not be ready for at least three months.

A working group has been established, but its recommendations will have to be ratified by the Chief Constables' Council in October. Even then, local police forces will not have to follow the " seize and warn " policy. So for the next year, there will still be what has been called a " post code lottery " on the laws. Where you are and especially who you are will still determine what the law is. That is absurd.
See
Wide Range Of Consequences For People Caught with Cannabis in UK.

However, the London police may not wait even until October. They are expected to roll out an extension of the Brixton experiment to the rest of the city soon.

This will eliminate what I call the " Needle Park syndrome " in which the problems of prohibition are concentrated in one area of tolerance. Some critics of the Brixton experiment have complained that the publicity around the zone of tolerance has brought more people into the area looking for cannabis, and other drugs. There does not seem to be much evidence of this, but formally extending the non-arrest policy to the rest of the city makes sense.
See

And will at least take the focus away from Brixton, which has many other problems.
See

It is likely that most of the cities in the England and Wales will follow the " seize and warn " policy because they have such severe hard drugs problems that they will have no choice. Scotland, which has a degree of autonomy in law enforcement, has already indicated that this will be its policy.
See

Now, where does this leave the UK's burgeoning cannabis café movement?

As a part of his " me-no-soft-on-drugs " posturing in his speech to Parliament Blunkett said, " Anyone attempting to open so-called " cannabis-cafes ", which either supply or allow the use of cannabis on their premises, will continue to break the law. The government would expect the police to respond swiftly and effectively to any such attempt to defy the law. "

That seems clear enough, but why should anyone believe him?

Even before his formal policy announcement the police have not really tried to close the Dutch Experience or the one or two other shops that have opened in England, although they have been raided. Moving to close them now will only raise the stakes and the issues that the Blair government does not want to recognize. Moreover, by delaying the change in the laws, while calling for a change in police policies, Blunkett is, whether he realizes it or not, " going Dutch " -- although not far enough.

In The Netherlands, possession and sale of cannabis are still technically illegal, but tolerated under guidelines conceptually similar to the interim polices to be formulated by the UK police, although very different in crucial details.

Moreover Dutch coffee shop policies are actually controlled locally and not nationally. Why can't the local UK police departments have similar policies for cannabis cafés, as appears to be the case in Stockport? In short, by leaving the law intact for a year, while changing de facto policies, Blunkett has left the situation very fluid, and has created a precedent for tolerating cannabis cafés.

As I said, there was no consideration or input from the cannabis community for these new regulations. Indeed, the principle justification used for these supposedly new policies, which grew out of actual police practices, was to increase police efficiency. Such traditional Anglo-Saxon concepts such as individual freedom and limited government had nothing to do with them, and it shows. This is truly offensive and should be of concern to everyone.

The fact is that British law enforcement is in crisis, in large part because of drug prohibition. Seventy percent of all UK prisoners and almost all women prisoners -- are locked up because of prohibition related crimes.

And just today, Cherie Blair, the Prime Minister's wife, who is a prominent attorney, made a speech deploring the overcrowding of UK prisons. The prison population stands at a record 71,360 just 293 short of its capacity.

This was not exactly new news. However, coming from so prominent a source, just as Blunkett sought to increase the penalties for selling cannabis, it added to the absurdity of the proposal.
See

In her speech, " The Law, The Victims and The Vulnerable ", Ms Blair said: " It is particularly worrying that more than one in six of the current prison population is on remand in other words they have yet to be tried or sentenced. In fact, the majority of this group doesn't ultimately go on to receive a prison sentence. "

That particularly applies to Colin Davies, but Ms Blair has probably never heard of him.

Someone else the Blairs may never have heard of is Raymond Nimmo, who won a £40,000 award last month in a lawsuit against his doctors for getting him addicted to Valium. After 14 years, he found out that all of his supposed medical problems were really caused by the " treatment. " According to The Observer, he is part of the 1.5 million Britons addicted to benzodiazepines.

These drugs are responsible for more deaths per year in Britain than cocaine, heroin and methadone combined.

Is that the proper classification for cannabis? Does it kill more people every year than all the hard drugs combined??

After all, Blunkett told Parliament that, according to " medical experts " on Parliament's Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs, " the current classification of cannabis is disproportionate in relation to the harm that it causes. "

That will still be true after it is reclassification.

If the Blair government came away from this exercise looking craven and incompetent, it ironic that is in large part due to their fear of criticism by the Tories, who managed to make even greater fools of themselves. That has been their track record on cannabis for some time.
See

As Edmund Burke, the great 18th century Tory, said of people like the current Conservative Party leadership, " They defend their errors as if they were defending their inheritance. "

First, on June 30th, Oliver Letwin, the Tory Shadow Home Secretary, (justice critic) attacked the Brixton experiment for supposedly giving control of the streets to " drug gangs " by saying, " There seems to be every evidence of these gangs and dealers dragging people on from cannabis to other drugs. "

That may be a new version of the " gateway! " Now people are being dragged through it. Of course, far from there being " every evidence " for this, there does not appear to be any evidence at all. In any case, this would be an argument for legalization.

It is sad to watch someone like Letwin, who is obviously intelligent and who claims to believe in liberty and who was one of eight Tory shadow ministers who admitted two years ago that they had " experimented " with cannabis in their youth -- sink to such malicious demagoguery.

He then compounded the Tories problems by taking their hapless party leader, Ian Duncan Smith, to a Baptist Church meeting in Brixton, which was a media disaster.

Letwin asked one mother: " Have you come across a situation where young people go from soft to hard drugs. " She replied: " No, that doesn't happen. "

Even if they are dragged??

These " community representatives " consisted of seven elderly women, two women under 60 one of them a vicar and a male youth worker, who turned out to be a Liberal Democrat Party member who supports liberalizing the cannabis laws. So much for the future of the Conservative Arrest Our Youth Party!

In fact, a poll taken by The Police Federation of 2,055 Lambeth residents showed 83% either supported the experiment outright or conditionally. Contrary to some reports, this support comes from all races. Only 7% of white people, 10% of black people, and 7% of Asian people were absolutely against it.

A nationwide Guardian/ICM poll taken in October of last year showed that 54% of Britons approved of reclassifying cannabis from a class B to a class C drug. Support rises to 65% among the 25 to 34 age group.

This polling data makes the stupid demagoguery of the Tories and the timid half-measures proposed by the Blair government all the more contemptible. As usual, " the leaders " are not leading.

The net result is a policy that is inherently unstable. Any realistic and humane cannabis policy has to provide for a legal supply.

Frankly, I doubt if this " new policy " will last until next July, when it is supposed to be enacted into law. By delaying the formal change for a year, Blunkett has insured that the issue will remain high on the public agenda, and that is the one thing that cannabis prohibition cannot survive.

We really are winning!
